messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Film Director
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Distraction: I distract myself with something else
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

Vignette:
Arthur is a 52-year-old film director who, until six months ago, was known for his calm authority on set and his meticulous visual style. That sense of control shattered during a night shoot for his latest feature. He was orchestrating a complex scene in a warehouse when a high-pitched groan of tortured metal cut through the air, followed by a concussive roar as a massive lighting rig tore free from the ceiling. The world was plunged into absolute blackness, filled with the sounds of crashing equipment, shattering bulbs, and panicked screams. Though he escaped with only minor physical injuries, the man who walked off that set was not the same one who had walked on.

The memory doesn’t arrive as a story he can tell. When his partner asks what happened, the words jam in his throat. He finds he can’t seem to put the frightening event into any kind of coherent narrative. Instead, it lives in him as a series of silent, searing Polaroids: the web of sparks cascading from the ceiling, the twisted metal frame just feet from where he stood, the chalky dust hanging in the air when the emergency lights finally flickered on. These images are perfectly, horribly clear, intruding without warning when he’s driving, or trying to fall asleep. To keep them at bay, he throws himself into anything else. He spends hours in his home editing suite, not working on a new project, but endlessly re-cutting old footage, the familiar hum of the machinery a shield against the silence where the pictures live.

His relationship with the world, especially the world of filmmaking he once commanded, is now governed by a pervasive sense of threat. On his last project, a short commercial he took on just to stay busy, he found himself unable to watch the actors, his gaze perpetually drifting upward to the scaffolding and light grids. He was superalert, cataloging every creak and groan of the building, certain that disaster was imminent. The sharp clap of the slate board, a sound he’d heard a million times, sent a jolt through him so violent he knocked over a monitor. The crew exchanged concerned glances, and in that moment, Arthur felt a profound sense of shame. He saw their looks as confirmation of a belief that had been hardening inside him: his reactions since the event showed he was a lousy coper.

This belief has reshaped his life. He began making excuses to avoid dailies in the dark screening rooms, claiming he preferred to review footage at home. The truth was, being in the dark now felt suffocating, a prelude to chaos. He has started to think constantly about why the event happened to him, replaying the day in his mind, searching for a sign he missed, a corner he cut. He was the director; the safety of the set was his ultimate responsibility. The thought has become a conviction: he is inadequate, a failure who let his people down. This new self—jumpy, avoidant, and riddled with self-doubt—is a stranger to him. "I don't even know who this person is anymore," he admitted to his partner last week, after startling violently at the sound of a pot lid clattering in the kitchen.

Arthur sought therapy after his agent called, concerned that he had turned down two promising feature films in a row. The thought of being in charge of another large-scale production, of being responsible for the safety of a hundred people under a ceiling of heavy equipment, was unbearable. He feels he has become unrecognisable to himself, a hollowed-out version of the confident man he once was. His greatest fear is that the director is gone for good, replaced by this watchful, frightened man who jumps at shadows and sounds.
